pages.x: In the 1920s America boomed. Cars, radios and refrigerators poured from its factories, and millions bought shares, often with borrowed money, sure that prices would keep rising. But farmers were struggling, wages lagged behind profits, and much of the boom ran on credit.

In late October 1929 share prices on the New York Stock Exchange collapsed. On Black Tuesday, 29 October, panicking traders sold 16 million shares. Fortunes vanished in days, and by 1932 the market had lost almost nine tenths of its value.

Banks failed by the thousand, taking people's savings with them, and factories closed. Families lost their homes and lived in shacks in camps they called Hoovervilles, after the president, Herbert Hoover, and queued for bread and soup.
pages.of: American workers had no job by 1933

pages.x: American banks called in their loans abroad, and countries put up tariffs to protect their own industries, so world trade shrank by two thirds. In Germany, still paying for the last war, six million were out of work by 1932. Desperate voters turned to extremes, and in 1933 Adolf Hitler came to power.

Franklin D. Roosevelt, elected in 1932, told Americans that the only thing they had to fear was fear itself. His New Deal put millions to work building dams, roads and parks, protected people's bank savings, and began pensions for the old. Recovery was slow, and only the Second World War ended the slump.

On the southern Great Plains, years of drought turned ploughed-up prairie to dust. Huge black storms buried farms and blew dust as far as the Atlantic. Hundreds of thousands of families packed up and drove west to California, where they picked fruit for pennies, as John Steinbeck told in The Grapes of Wrath.

In 1936 the photographer Dorothea Lange, working for the government, stopped at a camp of pea pickers in California and took a few pictures of a worn-out mother of seven, Florence Owens Thompson, with her children. It became the face of the Depression.

The Depression changed how governments think: most now accept that they must act to fight unemployment and protect savings in a crisis, as the economist John Maynard Keynes argued. It also showed how hard times can drive people to dictators, a lesson learned at terrible cost.
